content: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological condition that impacts millions of individuals globally. Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) are the primary treatment used to prevent seizures and manage epilepsy. While AEDs are effective in most cases, their long-term use is associated with adverse effects, including cognitive and behavioral changes. Therefore, when epilepsy enters remission, discontinuing AEDs may be beneficial for the patient. However, the ideal timing for stopping AEDs remains uncertain. This review is an updated version of the original Cochrane review published in 2001. The objectives of this review were as follows: 1. To measure and compare the risks of seizure recurrence, status epilepticus, and mortality following early versus late AED withdrawal in both adult and pediatric epilepsy patients. 2. To identify variables that influence the risk of seizure recurrence. 3. To determine a subgroup of patients for whom early AED withdrawal is safe. The search strategy included a comprehensive review of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to June 2014. Reference lists of identified studies were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated AED withdrawal after different durations of seizure remission in adults and children with epilepsy. Early AED withdrawal was defined as occurring after less than two years of seizure remission, while late withdrawal was defined as occurring after more than two years of remission. Two independent authors extracted data and assessed the quality of the included trials. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for each trial, and pooled RRs were determined using a fixed-effect model. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed for each pooled calculation. The risk of bias for each study was evaluated based on Cochrane Handbook guidelines, and the overall quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE system, with findings summarized in two tables. The review included five trials involving 924 randomized children with epilepsy, all under 16 years of age at the time of randomization, with a median follow-up period of 5.6 years. No eligible trials included adults or evaluated mortality or status epilepticus as outcomes. The pooled risk ratio for seizure relapse after AED withdrawal was 1.34 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.59, P = 0.0007). This indicates that early AED withdrawal increases the risk of seizure relapse. The number needed to harm (NNH), or the number of individuals exposed to early withdrawal to result in one additional seizure relapse, was calculated as 8 (95% CI 5 to 20). Early AED withdrawal was associated with higher relapse rates in individuals with partial seizures, with a pooled risk ratio of 1.51 (95% CI 0.97 to 2.35, P = 0.07). In contrast, individuals with absence-type epilepsy demonstrated a lower risk of relapse. Factors associated with an increased risk of seizure relapse included abnormal EEG findings (pooled RR 1.44, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.83, P = 0.003), particularly epileptiform activity (RR 2.58, 95% CI 2.03 to 3.28, P < 0.0001); epilepsy onset before the age of 2 years or after the age of 10 years; a history of status epilepticus; intellectual disability (IQ < 70); and high seizure frequency before and during treatment. Gender and family history did not significantly influence the risk of seizure relapse. The included trials were generally classified as having a low or unclear risk of bias, particularly when methodological details were not reported or could not be obtained from the original study authors. The authors concluded that there is evidence supporting the recommendation to wait at least two seizure-free years before discontinuing AEDs in children, especially in those with abnormal EEG findings or partial seizures, or both. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine the optimal timing for AED withdrawal in children with generalized seizures. Furthermore, no evidence is available to guide AED withdrawal timing in seizure-free adults. High-quality RCTs, particularly those involving adults and individuals with generalized seizure types, are needed to establish the best timing for AED withdrawal and to identify risk factors for seizure relapse.
